title: Pensacola Kid's pool hustling and the song 'Keep a-Knockin''
summary: Pensacola Kid hustled pool in towns, turned up running a Chicago pool hall, and claimed authorship of 'Keep a-Knockin''; the interviewers clarify he was a violinist.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah. He used to play pool, around Shreeport. And Pensacola kid would come into town like Alexander, you see, and he'd find out who's the best pool player in town and he'd lay around for a big game, you see. And when he'd get that big game, he'd fixin' to leave there then, you know, about $150 or two, $300. He's going to win that. He'd make the ball any way he want, any time, steal it, anything. And so when he left Alexander, he disappeared and we went to Chicago. We found him there running a pool hall for a fellow.

But that guy is a really violent player. And that tune come out, you know, about keep a knockin' and you can't come in, you know. I heard that thing before, you know. I heard it and I said, I know that piece. I've heard that somewhere. And I met him, you know. He told me that was by him. He made that piece. I didn't believe it. But I found out later that it was a hit to him. There ain't nothin' to it, but it was a hit. Everybody liked it.
Do you know any of the words to it?
No, I didn't know anymore. Keep knockin' and you can't come in. It's a kind of a spoody song, you know.
And they called, that was Paul Weyer, the violin player. Paul Weyer. They called him Pensacola Kid.
Pensacola Kid. Did he play piano?
I thought Pensacola Kid was a pianist. No, he was a violin.
